article.articleHeadline: Ebola death toll in the Democratic Republic of the Congo rises to 3,833.
article.articleSummary:
- Ebola in the Democratic Republic of the Congo continues to drive a high fatality burden. The DRC Ministry of Health reports that as of 24 September 2026, Ebola has caused 3,833 deaths among 7,946 confirmed infections, yielding a case fatality rate of 48.2%. These official numbers reflect ongoing outbreak activity in the country, with nearly half of confirmed cases resulting in death. The report provides counts of confirmed infections and deaths but does not include regional breakdowns, symptom details, laboratory confirmation methods, transmission sources, or information on imported or exported cases. The update highlights the severity of the outbreak in the DRC and the ongoing need for surveillance, public health measures, and response efforts.

Ursula von der Leyen disclosed at the UN General Assembly in New York that about 380 million euros will support Sub-Saharan Africa, targeting migrant protection and voluntary reintegration; a further 252 million euros will provide emergency assistance to communities impacted by conflicts, displacements, epidemics, and natural disasters. Distribution includes 97 million to Sub-Saharan Africa, 103 million to the Palestinian territories and Lebanon, and 52 million to Ukraine, aimed at winter preparedness. - As of 26 September 2026, Influenza Type A causes abrupt respiratory illness, typically heavier than seasonal flu, with most cases improving at home within about a week. Symptoms are described as sudden and may include fever and body aches; duration generally 3–7 days. Risk factors include close contact with infected individuals, immunocompromise, chronic diseases (asthma, diabetes, heart disease), and age groups under 5 or over 65. Management emphasizes rest and fluids; paracetamol or ibuprofen can relieve fever and pain. Antivirals such as oseltamivir or zanamivir may be prescribed for more severe cases. Transmission occurs via droplets and contaminated hands. Prevention: stay home when ill, wear masks in crowds, ensure ventilation, avoid crowded closed spaces, and practice hand hygiene.

article.articleHeadline: Editorial: Dengue vaccine, new hope against the disease.
article.articleSummary: Dengue remains a major public health challenge in India, with seasonal outbreaks across urban and rural areas driven by climate variability, urbanization, water stagnation, and mosquito breeding. Takeda's Qdenga dengue vaccine, in partnership with Hyderabad-based Dr. Reddy's Laboratories, will be promoted and distributed in the private Indian market, with a potential launch in the first half of 2027 pending local regulatory and commercial clearances; price details are not yet disclosed. Public affordability and broad access are key, as dengue affects not only megacities but smaller towns and rural communities. A long-term goal is to include Qdenga in India's public vaccination program, subject to disease burden, efficacy, safety, age groups, cost-effectiveness, and health-system impact. The rollout also aims to raise dengue awareness and engage health professionals; vaccination should complement, not replace, fundamental control measures such as vector control, sanitation, timely diagnosis, and proper treatment.

article.articleSummary: On 2026-09-26, Puducherry Chief Minister N. Rangasamy inaugurated a three-day National Conclave on Advanced Genomic Diagnostics for Tuberculosis and Policy Dialogue on Universal Drug Susceptibility Testing (UDST) using Targeted Next-Generation Sequencing (TNGS) for TB, organized by JIPMER. The national programme brought together policymakers, public health experts, clinicians, researchers and genomic scientists to deliberate on strengthening drug-resistance detection and advancing genomic technologies for TB diagnosis and treatment. The initiative focuses on scaling UDST through targeted sequencing to rapidly identify drug-resistant TB strains and guide therapy. Rangasamy stated that the Puducherry Government, in collaboration with the Centre, is undertaking several measures toward TB elimination. The conclave highlights the integration of advanced genomics into TB control efforts and reinforces policy dialogue and investment in diagnostics and treatment.

article.articleHeadline: Five months after elephant calf's anthrax death in MP, Bandhavgarh steps up surveillance
article.articleSummary: Gayatri, a four-year-old female elephant calf at Tala Camp, Bandhavgarh Tiger Reserve, Madhya Pradesh, died April 28 with symptoms suggestive of anthrax; lab confirmation by SWFH, Jabalpur, made it MP’s first confirmed wild-elephant anthrax death. Five months later, during Bandhavgarh’s five-day Hathi Mahotsava, 15 captive-trained elephants remain under round-the-clock monitoring. Precautions included cremation of Gayatri without autopsy, relocation of Tala camp elephants, quarantine and fencing of the death site, destruction of contaminated material, and vaccination of all 15 elephants after vaccines were obtained from Bengaluru with help from a Bhopal lab; staff received prophylactic antibiotics. Umaria district launched a bovine vaccination drive in villages adjoining the Tala core zone to reduce cross-species transmission. Anthrax spores persist in soil for decades, underpinning the long-term risk and need for SOPs and surveillance. The episode joins a history of wildlife anthrax outbreaks in India, such as Similipal (2016) and Dehing Patkai (2020).

article.articleHeadline: Pets battle tick uptick in rainy season
article.articleSummary: Kolkata reports a spike in tick fever among pets, including strays, as humid monsoon rains create ideal tick breeding conditions. Ehrlichiosis and Babesiosis are highlighted as consequential forms of tick fever; if not treated, infections can become complicated and lead to secondary problems. Fleas can carry tapeworms that are transmitted by bites. Monsoon-focused care includes daily grooming, regular hydration, and cooked meals, plus routine health checks and tick-control with sprays or tablets; there is no vaccine for this condition. Pet parents should monitor for redness, itching, rashes, hair loss or unpleasant odour and seek veterinary advice. Reports come from Kolkata, including New Alipore and Belgachhia Veterinary Hospital.

article.articleHeadline: RIPK2 Inhibitor GSK583 Curbss H1N1 Flu Replication and Tames Lung
article.articleSummary: Influenza A/H1N1 PR8 (A/Puerto Rico/8/1934) replication was curtailed by RIPK2 inhibitor GSK583 in vitro and in a mouse infection model conducted by teams at the University of Science and Technology of China and Huazhong University of Science and Technology. In cell culture, GSK583 reduced viral RNA and viral protein, and supernatants yielded far fewer plaque-forming units, indicating suppression of virion release rather than direct inactivation or receptor-blocking. Time-of-addition experiments showed activity only after adsorption, consistent with post-entry effects or host signaling. In mice treated early after infection, disease severity was alleviated, pulmonary viral RNA and nucleoprotein were reduced, and lung inflammation declined, signaling lower replication and tissue damage. Mechanistically, the RIPK2–MKK7–JNK axis underlies the effect: RIPK2–MKK7 interaction and JNK phosphorylation tracked with replication, and genetic or pharmacologic disruption of this axis corroborated the findings. This host-directed approach could broaden influenza therapeutics and reduce severe lung injury.

article.articleHeadline: Mycoplasma Leads Pediatric Respiratory Infections in Post-COVID China,
article.articleSummary: In Ningbo, Zhejiang Province, China, a retrospective analysis of 34,404 pediatric patients with respiratory symptoms (Jan 2023–Dec 2024) found Mycoplasma pneumoniae as the leading positive pathogen at 26.94%, making it the top cause of pediatric respiratory infections. Throat swabs were tested with multiplex PCR for 13 viral and atypical bacterial pathogens, yielding an overall positivity rate of 69.14%. Rhinovirus was second (16.29%), adenovirus third (9.00%). Coinfections occurred in 19.85% of positive samples, with dual infections most common. Seasonal variation was evident over the two-year period, highlighting rebound patterns after COVID-19 restrictions eased. Mycoplasma pneumoniae, an atypical bacterium lacking a cell wall, does not respond to beta-lactams, underscoring implications for treatment decisions. Findings from the Affiliated Women and Children’s Hospital of Ningbo University and published in BMC Infectious Diseases provide an epidemiological reference for post-COVID pediatric respiratory care and testing strategies.

article.articleHeadline: Gut Microbe's Acetate Signal Calms Deadly Diarrhea in Newborn Calves
article.articleSummary: Published in Microbiome on 2026-09-26, Huazhong Agricultural University researchers trace a microbiota–metabolite–immune axis in neonatal calf diarrhea. Diarrheic newborn calves show gut dysbiosis, metabolic perturbation, and inflammatory activation. Fecal microbiota transplantation from healthy calves alleviates diarrhea and coincides with enrichment of Bifidobacterium pseudocatenulatum and higher fecal acetate. In vitro, live B. pseudocatenulatum increases acetate production, suggesting a causal bacterium–metabolite link. In murine models mimicking calf intestinal injury, treatment with live B. pseudocatenulatum or acetate reduces intestinal damage and pathogen-driven Th17/IL-17A responses; heat-killed bacteria lose protection, implicating microbial metabolism. Acetate signals via FFAR2, and FFAR2 blockade attenuates protection. These findings define a targetable microbiota–metabolite–immune pathway with potential probiotic or metabolite-based interventions for neonatal calf diarrhea.

article.articleHeadline: Online reports of a 'massive outbreak' of syphilis in Japan draw attention; Lion City government: Singapore's incidence rate has fallen for three consecutive years - Local - Lion City: Two or Three Things
article.articleSummary: Syphilis remains a public health concern across Asia. In Japan, official data show cases peaked around 15,000 in 2023 and have since declined; however, a shortage of Pfizer’s long-acting benzathine penicillin is expected to persist until the second half of next year. Singapore reports a three-year decline in syphilis incidence, from 129 per 100,000 in 2022 to 107 (2023), 86 (2024), and 84 (2025), with benzathine penicillin supplies currently sufficient. The infection is mainly transmitted via unprotected sex, blood, and mother-to-child transmission, not casual contact. Measures include increased sampling of migratory bird droppings, poultry farms, and surrounding environments; reinforced cleaning and disinfection of high-risk areas and farm biosecurity, especially anti-bird facilities; and intensified cleaning/disinfection checks of egg cartons. High-risk districts in Tainan—Xiaying, Liujia, Beimen, Xigang, Jiali, Guantian, Houbi, Madou, Xuejia, Yanshui and nearby wetlands—will see expanded surveillance across land poultry farms, duck farms, and goose farms. article.articleHeadline: "Raising bricks" is very therapeutic? Doctor: Do not ignore the health risks posed by fungi.
article.articleSummary: “Raising bricks” in Jiangsu, China, a low-cost stress-relief trend involving damp bricks with moss, raises health concerns as users report sneezing, runny nose, and itchy eyes. Jiangsu Provincial People’s Hospital ENT physician Wang Yunli explains moist moss on bricks creates an ideal host for fungi such as Aspergillus; inhaled spores can trigger allergic rhinitis and allergic conjunctivitis, with symptoms including paroxysmal sneezing, watery rhinorrhea, nasal itching, obstruction, and eye itching/redness. In immunocompromised individuals, fungi may colonize and invade, causing invasive fungal infections of the respiratory tract, lungs, or brain. Fungal sinusitis may present with foul odor and dark secretions seen after surgical access to sinuses. Skin contact can cause dermatitis or infection if skin is breached; brick surfaces may carry tetanus bacillus, Legionella, or Staphylococcus. Precautions include ventilated placement, masks during handling, hand washing, and saline nasal irrigation; those with allergies, asthma, or immune suppression should avoid. Humid areas near Nanjing have higher fungal prevalence.

article.articleHeadline: Hong Kong officials investigate human infection of rat Hepatitis E virus

His blood sample tested positive for rat HEV by the Public Health Laboratory Services Branch, CHP. Symptoms were relatively mild and he was discharged on 21 September after treatment. Rat HEV infections in humans mainly affect immunocompromised individuals; most cases are asymptomatic, while symptomatic patients may experience fatigue, abdominal pain and loss of appetite, with jaundice being less common. Transmission routes include ingestion of food or water contaminated by rodents or their excreta, exposure to contaminated environments/objects, and direct contact with rodents. Prevention emphasizes personal, food and environmental hygiene, the Five Keys to Food Safety, and rodent-control measures to reduce contact.

article.articleHeadline: Highly Pathogenic Avian Influenza: What Kind of Infectious Disease Is It? Key Points to Keep in Mind — Asahi Shimbun
article.articleSummary: Highly Pathogenic Avian Influenza (HPAI) is an A-type influenza virus that primarily infects birds. Pathogenicity differs by poultry strain: low-pathogenic forms cause mild or no symptoms, while high-pathogenic forms trigger systemic illness and can wipe out flocks within days. The virus's surface is defined by two glycoproteins, hemagglutinin (HA) and neuraminidase (NA); to date, 18 HA subtypes and 11 NA subtypes have been identified, with combinations creating multiple subtypes, including H5N1, a representative high-pathogenic strain. H5N1 was first identified in 1996 in Guangdong Province, China. The article notes the worldwide spread of highly pathogenic avian influenza, with infections now seen in a range of mammalian species, underscoring cross-species transmission concerns. The piece emphasizes understanding these molecular features and subtypes to grasp ongoing outbreaks as of the published date, 2026-09-27.

article.articleHeadline: Hunger Hormone Receptor Emerges as Unexpected Lever Against Parasitic Liver
article.articleSummary: Cystic echinococcosis of the liver due to Echinococcus granulosus progressed more with ghrelin signaling. In Xinjiang, China, infected mice treated for 90 days showed that ghrelin administration raised serum ghrelin and hepatic ghrelin/GHSR, increased proliferation markers (Ki67, PCNA, Cyclin D1/E1), and suppressed the TGF-β1/Smad3 fibrotic pathway, reducing fibrosis proteins (α-SMA, Collagen I/III) and accelerating parasite growth. Blocking GHSR with the antagonist [D-Lys3]-GHRP-6 produced the opposite: lower ghrelin signaling, fewer proliferation signals, activation of TGF-β1/Smad3, higher fibrotic proteins, and a tighter fibrotic capsule around the cyst with slowed infection progression. Thus, fibrosis here acts as a containment wall, constraining the parasite. Ghrelin signaling emerges as a potential therapeutic target for a disease with limited drug options. Endemic in Central Asia, the Middle East, South America, and parts of China; Acta Parasitologica, 2026.

article.articleHeadline: World Rabies Day on September 28: China CDC reminds that bats and other animals can also transmit rabies

Viral genome sequencing showed the cat’s virus highly homologous to a canine strain, suggesting dog-to-cat transmission prior to human exposure. In China, about 5% of rabies cases arise from cat bites or scratches. The China CDC emphasizes rabies as a zoonotic disease with near 100% fatality once symptoms appear, yet prevention via vaccination and prompt post-exposure prophylaxis is highly effective. Public guidance: vaccinate dogs and cats annually, seek immediate medical care after bites or scratches, and complete prescribed prophylaxis. Note: bats can transmit rabies; avoid handling them.

article.articleHeadline: Measles cases in Manokwari rise; Health Office to conduct mass supplementary immunization in October 2026.
article.articleSummary: Measles cases in Manokwari, West Papua, have prompted a rapid public health response. Through mid-September 2026, 70 suspected measles cases were recorded across eight Puskesmas jurisdictions, with three laboratory-confirmed positives at Wosi, Sanggeng, and Pasir Putih clinics. Of the suspects, 47 cases (67%) are under five years old, and 49 cases (70%) lack immunization evidence, indicating gaps in vaccination coverage. Thirty-four patients (49%) required hospitalization at RSUD Manokwari or RSUP, though the Case Fatality Rate stands at 0%. A cluster in Kampung Susweni (Amban Puskesmas) yielded 13 cases within 20 days, signaling active household transmission. Epidemiologists note that Manokwari meets the criteria for a public health emergency (KLB) with 28 cases from weeks 31–36. Outbreak Response Immunization (ORI) for Measles-Rubella will run for 12 working days, Oct 5–17, 2026, targeting 9 months to under 5 years with at least 95% coverage, preceded by socialization Sept 28–Oct 3.

article.articleHeadline: Don't Always Assume It's Just a Cold; Coughing Could Be a Symptom of Pneumonia.
article.articleSummary: Indonesia faces pneumonia awareness gaps as coughing is often treated as a common cold. A YouGov survey cited in the article found 41% of Indonesian adults have never heard of pneumonia. The misconception of ‘paru-paru basah’ as night-time exposure rather than fluid buildup leads to delays in care. Diagnosis requires clinical evaluation and laboratory tests; early outpatient care is insufficient in high-risk groups. People over 60, and those with diabetes, asthma, cardiovascular disease, or stroke history, should seek urgent evaluation if symptoms persist beyond 3–4 days, or if there is severe dyspnea or sudden confusion.

article.articleHeadline: Symptoms of the Super Flu and When to See a Doctor
article.articleSummary: On 26 September 2026, Indonesian health authorities clarify that the term 'Super Flu' does not correspond to a distinct medical disease. It refers to Influenza A infections; however, World Health Organization and the U.S. CDC do not recognize 'Super Flu' as a separate condition. There is no clinical evidence that Influenza A is more dangerous than other influenza strains. Because Influenza A symptoms closely resemble other acute respiratory infections, distinguishing it without testing is challenging. Definitive identification requires laboratory confirmation, such as antigen swab tests or a PCR panel. The article emphasizes seeking medical care when appropriate, and points to a video that discusses symptoms and when to see a doctor. The discussion originates from Indonesia's Ministry of Health statements by Aji Muhawarman, noting the need for lab tests to determine the circulating virus.

article.articleHeadline: Global analysis maps Staphylococcus aureus burden and antibiotic resistance
article.articleSummary: Staphylococcus aureus accounts for about a quarter of bovine intramammary infections (mastitis) globally, drawn from 143 studies (2010–2025) across 40 countries. Global prevalence estimated at 24.78% (95% CI 21.27–28.47), with Africa 29.21%, North America 28.15%, Asia 25.88%, Europe 14.19%, and Oceania 5.27%. Country-level highs include Cameroon 67%, Sri Lanka 64.32%, Indonesia 56.98%, Mexico 48%, Japan 47.44%, Uruguay 47.07%; lows include Poland 0.70%, Australia 5.49%, New Zealand 5.32%. Prevalence rose through 2014–2018, peaking in 2018 (41.39%), with recent years often higher, possibly due to improved surveillance and larger dairy herds. Antimicrobial resistance is alarmingly high: penicillin 65.19%, ampicillin 62.80%, amoxicillin 52.07%; doxycycline 70.73%, oxytetracycline 62.42%; oxacillin 40.23% and vancomycin 44.62% show notable resistance. Resistance genes blaZ, mecA, ermC/B, msrA, mphC, tetK/L/M are common, frequently carried on mobile elements, signaling multidrug resistance and challenging mastitis control.

The integrated system consolidates data from the Early Warning and Response System (SKDR), the National Animal Health Information System (ISIKHNAS), and the SehatSatli platform to support monitoring of diseases in humans, domestic animals, and wildlife. This One Health approach strengthens collaboration among human health, animal health, and wildlife health sectors, enabling more coordinated detection, reporting, and rapid response to zoonoses and new infections tied to wildlife and conservation ecosystems, and helps prevent spillover to humans.

MDPP education has reached 178,358 people across Balekambang and Pekayon (East Jakarta) and Pengadegan and Pejaten Timur (South Jakarta). The initiative uses the motto 'One House, One Jumantik, Zero Larvae' and involves Dinas Kesehatan and partners.

article.articleHeadline: Prevent TB from Spreading, Cirebon Expands Tracing Up to 412 Villages | Republika Online
article.articleSummary: Tuberculosis (TB) tracing in Cirebon Regency, Indonesia, is expanding to 412 villages under a free health-check program. By the third week of September 2026, Health Office staff had surveyed 340 of 412 villages. The integrated tracing targets contacts of TB patients, those with cough, and individuals with risk factors. Since early August, about 34,000 people in 340 villages were screened; of roughly 18,000 records entered, around 2,200 were categorized as suspected TB, with 74 confirmed positive and started on treatment. Family household members of patients (234) have also received treatment; tracing was extended around residences to identify additional transmission. The plan aims to screen 46,600 people (about 100 per village) through November 2026, using free screenings and mobile X-ray units. Nationwide TB control targets by 2030 seek a 50% reduction versus 2025, not zero cases.

article.articleHeadline: The challenge of finding a vaccine for the Ebola epidemic in the Democratic Republic of the Congo - 3CatInfo
article.articleSummary: In the Democratic Republic of the Congo, the Ebola epidemic—driven by the Bundibugyo strain—continues, marking the largest Bundibugyo outbreak with over 7,700 laboratory-confirmed cases and more than 3,700 deaths. A vaccine developed for Bundibugyo has begun Phase I safety testing, with field efficacy trials planned in DRC to test protection against this strain. A second trial starts using a vaccine approved for the Zaire strain to evaluate potential cross-protection and to safeguard frontline responders. WHO Africa Emergencies Director Marie Roseline Belizaire, speaking from Kinshasa, highlights the need to test vaccines in the outbreak setting, while MSF notes the importance of protecting health workers like those cited by Nana Mimbu. The outbreak has expanded from three to seven provinces in a conflict-affected, highly mobile mining region with a fragile health system and community distrust; international support remains essential.

article.articleHeadline: Artificial intelligence speeds up monitoring of the Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo.
article.articleSummary: Ebola outbreak monitoring in eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo is being accelerated by digital tools and AI. Despite difficult ground access, power and communications shortages, response teams rely on satellite links and mobile apps to transmit data. In June, Africa CDC announced Starlink delivered 150 satellite communication kits to Ituri to speed data transfer and field coordination. In September, CEPI convened Anthropic, WHO Africa, and the National Institute for Biomedical Research (INRB) to explore Claude, Anthropic’s AI assistant, for real-time data processing. Regions frequently send data via WhatsApp, which Claude ingests, consolidates, and compares to prior reports, highlighting changes. The daily reporting process has dropped from about a full day to under one hour. A reported 70 new confirmed Ebola cases in 24 hours underscores the need for rapid data analysis to guide outbreak control.

article.articleHeadline: Fantástico presents Sônia Bridi's series about the Ebola epidemic in Africa - Fala Canedo.

The series aims to inform and provoke action on how society can respond to Ebola and similar epidemics in Africa.

article.articleHeadline: DRC/Ebola: the government approves the new preparedness and response plan.
article.articleSummary: DRC approves a new 180-day multisectoral 'One Health' preparedness and response plan for Ebola virus disease caused by Bundibugyo ebolavirus, launched in September 2026. The plan provides a common reference framework for ongoing prevention and response activities and includes review of the current epidemiological situation, noting a downward trend in affected provinces except North Kivu, which continues to report cases. The government, via the Ministry of Health, also announces a phased rollout of free healthcare in Ituri for the duration of the Ebola outbreak, initially in Bunia and Rwampara, with expansion contingent on medicine and human-resource availability. By month’s end, partner-supplied medicines are expected to enable free-care in Ituri. Kinshasa is identified as a high-risk zone, prompting reinforced preparedness, and emphasis on engaging religious leaders to bolster community awareness and response.

article.articleHeadline: DRC: Hippos Found Dead in Virunga National Park

Experts recommend incinerating cadavers with controlled sites to prevent further contamination and to avoid burying them.

article.articleHeadline: 26/9 on Nieuwsuur: Ebola in the Congo • The Future of the UN
article.articleSummary: Bundibugyo variant of Ebola continues to spread in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC), with at least 3,799 deaths, primarily among young children, making it the deadliest Ebola outbreak on record. article.articleHeadline: Where do viruses hide after an epidemic ends? The mystery of the natural reservoir of one of the world's deadliest viruses.
article.articleSummary: Natural reservoirs of deadly viruses remain elusive; animal origins drive spillover. Nipah (Malaysia, 1998) traced to fruit bats; bat-contaminated fruit dropped on pig farms led to pig infections and human cases, with transmission to predominantly non-Muslim Chinese-origin workers; deforestation pushing bats toward orchards emphasized the need to separate pig enclosures from fruit trees. Ebola and related viruses have caused dozens of outbreaks in West and Central Africa over the past 50 years; an ongoing eastern Democratic Republic of Congo outbreak is the second-largest in history, with more than 7,400 cases and over 3,600 deaths. While bats remain a plausible reservoir for Ebola, evidence is lacking and no animal species has been confirmed as the reservoir. Detecting reservoirs relies on sampling apparently healthy animals to detect active virus, guiding prevention and public health measures.

article.articleHeadline: More than 34,000 dengue fever cases in Ho Chi Minh City: Be vigilant for warning signs.
article.articleSummary: Dengue fever remains high in Ho Chi Minh City (TP.HCM), with over 34,000 cases year-to-date as the city enters the rainy season that promotes Aedes breeding. In week 38 (Sept 14–20), TP.HCM recorded 1,462 dengue cases, bringing the total to 34,161 by week 38. High-incidence areas include Con Dao, Chanh Phu Hoa ward, and Minh Thanh. Dengue can progress severely in adults, especially those with underlying conditions. Warning signs needing urgent care include severe abdominal pain, persistent vomiting, unusual bleeding, or lethargy. There is no antiviral; treatment centers on rest, rehydration, symptom control, and close monitoring. The Qdenga vaccine, a live attenuated tetravalent vaccine covering DENV-1 to DENV-4, is approved in Vietnam for people aged 4 and older and is administered via Long Chau centers after clinician assessment—complementing, not replacing, vector control. Emphasize early detection and prevention: eliminate breeding sites, protect against bites, and consider vaccination where appropriate.

article.articleHeadline: Fever after returning from Southeast Asia during the Chuseok holiday? "Please get a dengue fever test" - Society | Hankook Ilbo
article.articleSummary: KDCA analysis of overseas dengue fever laboratory testing (2020–2025) shows 2,904 tests requested nationwide, with 613 positives (21.1%). Early pandemic years yielded few positives (39 positives, 6.4%); 2021 had only 3. From 2022, as international travel resumed, testing and confirmed infections rose: 2021 69 tests; 2022 338; 2023 632; 2024 900; 2025 757; positives: 2022 98; 2023 177; 2024 177; 2025 122. Among 568 cases with identifiable travel origins, 487 (85.7%) were infected after visiting Southeast Asia. Indonesia accounted for 124 cases (21.8%), the Philippines 110 (19.4%), Vietnam 110 (19.4%), and Thailand 71 (12.5%); together these four countries explain 73.1% of imported infections. Dengue is transmitted by Aedes mosquitoes; typical symptoms include high fever, headache, myalgia, arthralgia, and rash; about 75% are asymptomatic. Korea has no indigenous dengue, but imported cases are monitored as a Class 3 communicable disease. Travelers to Southeast Asia should wear long sleeves, use repellents, and seek testing if fever or related symptoms arise within two weeks of return, reporting travel history to clinicians.

article.articleHeadline: Foot-and-mouth disease: APPEC warns about the economic risk to meat exports.
article.articleSummary: Foot-and-mouth disease (FMD), especially serotype SAT 1, is framed by Paraguay’s APPEC as an economic threat to meat exports as SAT 1 spreads beyond its historical range. The World Organisation for Animal Health (WOAH) monitors SAT 1 incursions in Africa, Europe, the Middle East and Asia, signaling risks to animal health, livelihoods, food security and international trade. Economic losses can reach about 1% of GDP in small cattle-dependent economies, with trade disruptions potentially matching or exceeding direct production losses. In Paraguay, beef exports through August 2026 totaled 186,175 tonnes worth US$1.299 billion, down 25% in volume versus 2025, while the average price rose to US$7,410/ton. Main destinations included Chile (20,609 t, US$399 million), followed by Israel, the United States, Taiwan and Brazil. APPEC calls for stronger vaccination and epidemiological surveillance; WOAH emphasizes vaccination, biosecurity, movement controls, border surveillance and early warning systems. Paraguay also pursued new markets, such as beef shipments to the UAE and veterinary audits for Turkey.

article.articleHeadline: Dozens of whale calves die in Argentina, bacterial infection suspected
article.articleSummary: Dozens of southern right whale calves washed up dead along Argentina's Valdés Peninsula in northern Patagonia; a bacterial infection is the most likely cause, with the bacterium capable of causing systemic disease in calves. No evidence of human-caused factors. Investigations are underway with scientists, including CONICET. The affected species, southern right whales (Eubalaena australis), migrate to coasts of Argentina, Brazil and Uruguay to breed and raise young, with large numbers gathering in the gulf areas of northern Patagonia. A death toll is described as 'fairly high' by CONICET scientist Mariano Coscarella; officials caution that right whale mortality occurs annually and could reflect natural population dynamics. The main hypothesis mirrors outbreaks elsewhere; Valdés Peninsula spans about 4,000 sq km and is a UNESCO site, where nutrient-rich waters from two converging currents sustain breeding grounds for numerous marine mammals.

article.articleHeadline: Tucumán researchers developed a novel vaccine against intestinal infections.
article.articleSummary: Argentine researchers from Tucumán have developed an oral vaccine to protect against intestinal infections caused by Salmonella and Shigella. In a preclinical program, the vaccine uses a genetically modified, attenuated Salmonella strain administered orally as drops once a year, aimed at children, to elicit immunity against both pathogens. There are currently no vaccines to prevent gastrointestinal disease from Salmonella or Shigella; existing Salmonella vaccines target typhoid fever (Salmonella Typhi). The team seeks a single formulation covering both bacteria, with beta-glucan (fungal) studied as an adjuvant to boost the immune response. Early tests show beta-glucans do not affect bacterial viability for at least two months, allowing progression to formulation studies. INSIBIO—the joint institute of Universidad Nacional de Tucumán and CONICET—leads the work, with María Victoria Pacello and Mónica Alejandra Delgado. Results will be presented at AUGM in Porto Alegre, Brazil.

article.articleHeadline: Even with the worst epidemic of the decade, only 16.3% of doses against chikungunya were administered in Mato Grosso do Sul.
article.articleSummary: Mato Grosso do Sul, Brazil, recorded 31 chikungunya deaths and 10,367 confirmed cases in 2026, the worst outbreak of the decade. Vaccination remains limited: 64,452 doses were received, but only 10,494 were administered (16.3%) across six municipalities—Sete Quedas, Amambai, Douradina, Itaporã, Dourados, and Batayporã; Dourados led with 5,715 doses. The state also reported 119 pregnant women among cases, with one death under investigation. Total probable cases in 2026 reached 12,120, about 86% of 2025’s 14,100. El Niño conditions could fuel a new surge, as higher temperatures likely boost Aedes aegypti transmission, potentially extending into 2027. Chikungunya (CHIKV) is transmitted by infected female Aedes aegypti; symptoms include high fever and severe joint pain, with possible cardiovascular, renal, dermatological, and neurological complications. Diagnostic tests exist; vaccination stock remains in state and municipal networks.

triage.headline_ja: 10年で最悪の流行にもかかわらず、マットグロッソ・ド・スル州のチクングニアワクチン接種率はわずか16.3%
triage.triage_reason: ブラジル・マットグロッソ・ド・スル州で過去10年で最悪のチクングニア流行（31人死亡、1万人超の確定例）が発生しており、IHR基準（深刻な公衆衛生影響、異常性）を2つ満たすためフルリスク評価へ進めるべきと判断。
triage.notes: El Niño条件による気温上昇でAedes aegyptiの媒介活動が活発化し、2027年まで流行が延長する可能性が指摘されている。ワクチン接種率の低さ（16.3%）が今後の感染拡大リスクを高める要因。

article.articleHeadline: Hidden Viral Worlds and Antibiotic Resistance Genes Found in Colombian
article.articleSummary: Across seven Colombian sites in the Caribbean and Amazon, a metatranscriptomic survey of blood-feeding insects (Aedes, Culex, Psorophora, Coquillettidia, Lutzomyia, Psychodopygus) identified 416 viral sequences from 13 families in 23 RNA-seq libraries, dominated by insect-specific viruses rather than human pathogens. The researchers also mapped transcriptionally active bacterial microbiomes and antimicrobial resistance genes, confirming species by COI barcodes and using TPM normalization. Wolbachia appeared actively in Culex, Coquillettidia, and Aedes albopictus, underscoring its potential relevance for biocontrol. Low-abundance human-associated bacteria (Cutibacterium, Faecalibacterium, Prevotella, Hallela, Escherichia) likely reflect urban exposure and could serve as sentinels for environmental contamination and resistance gene flow. Virome composition varied markedly even among nearby pools, indicating ecological factors beyond host identity shape virus persistence. The findings stress the need for continuous, spatially distributed monitoring of vector microbiomes in dengue, Zika, chikungunya, and leishmaniasis burdened regions.

article.articleHeadline: Pocah declares her love to Arthur Pelágio after her boyfriend took care of his mother with chikungunya.
article.articleSummary: On September 26, 2026, Brazilian singer Pocah revealed on social media that her mother contracted chikungunya and needed care. Despite a demanding schedule—new project, concerts, endorsements, and exams—Pocah said she had to juggle responsibilities to look after her mother. She praised her boyfriend, Arthur Pelágio, for staying by their side, spending nights at the hospital, continuing to work without sleep, and providing emotional support and smiles during tense moments. The post underscores personal resilience and partner support amid illness, with no details on laboratory confirmation, infection source, or geographic spread. The report centers on familial strain and the caring role of a partner during a chikungunya infection, rather than epidemiology or public health response.

article.articleHeadline: DOH raises Code White alert for 'Queenie'
article.articleSummary: Severe Tropical Storm Queenie (international name Surigae) prompted the Philippines Department of Health to raise Code White to ensure rapid response. The DOH Operations Center remains on 24/7 alert, with Code White response teams, health commodities, and DOH hospital ERs on standby to address road accidents and health emergencies. The DOH is coordinating with the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Council, local government units, and regional disaster units as Queenie is expected to intensify into a typhoon but is not forecast to make landfall or directly affect the country. The storm is expected to bring rains and potential flooding; the public is urged to avoid wading through floodwaters to prevent leptospirosis and other diseases. If wading is unavoidable, seek medical attention at the nearest health facility or YAKAP clinic. Published 2026-09-26.

article.articleHeadline: DOH expands patient tracker as dengue, leptospirosis cases surge
article.articleSummary: Philippines' Department of Health (DOH) expanded its Leptospirosis Tracker into a Unified Leptospirosis and Dengue Case Tracker across DOH hospitals and partner government health facilities in response to rising dengue and leptospirosis activity. The system monitors hospital capacity, caseloads, referrals, and resource needs to support timely operational decisions. It tracks bed occupancy and clinical status to identify facilities at or near capacity, guiding patient referrals, surge measures, and resource augmentation. From Aug. 6–19 to Aug. 20–Sept. 2, leptospirosis cases more than doubled from 1,762 to 3,805, while dengue cases rose from 17,342 to 19,792. This reflects an approximate 116% increase for leptospirosis and about 14% for dengue. The expansion aims to improve coordination amid ongoing outbreaks in the Philippines.

article.articleHeadline: Enteric infections and childhood stunting: a systematic review and meta-analysis across four pathogen domains
article.articleSummary: Systematic review and meta-analysis across four pathogen domains links enteric infections with early childhood linear growth faltering and stunting in low- and middle-income countries. It draws on cohorts including Malawi (association between asymptomatic infections and growth impairment), rural Bangladesh (diarrheal illness and enteropathogen exposure), the Philippines (environmental enteric dysfunction and stunting), and Ethiopia (soil-transmitted helminths and intestinal protozoa). The analysis highlights pathogens such as Cryptosporidium and enteroaggregative Escherichia coli, as well as broader enteropathogen burdens detected by multiplex real-time PCR. Environmental enteric dysfunction and repeated enteric infections are implicated in impaired growth trajectories, underscoring the need for integrated nutrition, water, sanitation, and hygiene interventions and improved diagnostics in LMICs. Published 2026-09-26.

article.articleHeadline: Measles spike in Peru: cases doubled in a month and a half, and authorities warn they could quadruple.
article.articleSummary: Measles outbreak in Peru could worsen, with cases doubling from 1,236 on July 26 to about 2,400, according to health authorities. The Ministry of Health logged 1,747 confirmed cases in epidemiological week 33, while unofficial updates note rising totals. Puno leads with 1,264 cases, followed by Arequipa (292); Cusco and Madre de Dios also report cases. A 16-year-old unvaccinated resident of Alto Monte, San Pablo, Ramón Castilla, Loreto, died from measles complications including pneumonia—the country’s first measles death in 23 years. Experts warn cases could triple or quadruple in the next month, especially in the Amazon region with low vaccination coverage. Vaccination gaps are widening: first-dose coverage down ~80%, second-dose ~75%. About 50–60% of cases are 10–29 years old; in San Pablo, around 40% are 16–26. Coordinated government action, potentially an emergency declaration, is urged, as Loreto’s remote communities face access barriers.

article.articleHeadline: San Lazaro Hospital reports 40 deaths due to leptospirosis
article.articleSummary: Leptospirosis outbreak at San Lazaro Hospital in Manila, Philippines, with 40 deaths reported as of Sept. 24. The hospital noted a rising fatality toll this year, increasing from 24 deaths on Sept. 10 to 27 on Sept. 14 and 31 on Sept. 18, reaching 40. Overall admissions for leptospirosis reached 823. Of these, one patient is in intensive care and three are on hemodialysis. Dr. Rontgene Solante, head of adult infectious diseases and tropical medicine at SLH, said pulmonary hemorrhage is the most common cause of death in this outbreak, describing it as bleeding in the lungs. The Department of Health reported 10,936 suspected leptospirosis cases as of Sept. 16, a 38% increase from 7,931 cases in the same period in 2025, indicating a continuing surge.

article.articleHeadline: Dengue cases in Cam. Sur hit over 1,200; 18 dead
article.articleSummary: Dengue cases in Camarines Sur, Philippines, exceed 1,200 with 18 deaths as of 2026-09-27. Gov. Miguel Villafuerte mobilized provincial resources for prevention, surveillance, medical response, hospital preparedness, referral, and immediate action in areas with rising cases. The response prioritizes community-driven vector control: search and destroy mosquito breeding sites, prevent water stagnation, and keep water containers, yards, canals, schools, and workplaces clean. Residents are urged to seek medical care promptly if symptoms such as prolonged fever appear. No details on laboratory confirmation, infection source, or imported/exported cases are provided. The outbreak underscores local public health measures and coordinated action to curb dengue transmission in Camarines Sur, with ongoing vigilance required in affected communities.

article.articleHeadline: Namibia halts meat exports after rare foot-and-mouth disease outbreak
article.articleSummary: Namibia records its first outbreak of foot-and-mouth disease (FMD) in its primary commercial livestock zone in six decades, prompting a nationwide ban on livestock movement and meat exports. FMD is a highly contagious viral infection affecting cattle and other cloven-hoofed animals, not dangerous to humans. Namibia becomes the eighth southern African country to be hit by FMD this year, after Botswana, Eswatini, Lesotho, Mozambique, South Africa, Zambia and Zimbabwe. The virus breached Namibia's veterinary cordon fence, crossing from the endemic northern region into the south, an area that had remained officially FMD-free since 1964. Authorities have intensified surveillance, restricted animal movements, and halted meat exports to safeguard regional markets and prevent further spread.

article.articleHeadline: Zambia Calls for Stronger Pandemic Preparedness - ZNBC
article.articleSummary: Zambia calls for stronger global pandemic preparedness and cooperation to prevent and respond to future pandemics. Health Minister ROMA CHILENGI delivered Zambia's national statement at the United Nations High-Level Meeting on Pandemic Prevention, Preparedness and Response, speaking on behalf of President HAKAINDE HICHILEMA. Preparedness must be properly planned, financed and tested to ensure countries can respond effectively to health emergencies. Zambia commits to working with other Member States, the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention - Africa CDC -, the United Nations and the World Health Organization. The COVID-19 pandemic showed how a health emergency can quickly develop into an economic, social and development crisis, and exposed inequalities in access to vaccines, diagnostic services, medicines and other life-saving technologies. The experience calls for stronger global cooperation and fairer access to essential health products and technologies.

article.articleHeadline: Thailand Floods Spark Disease Warnings By Health Experts
article.articleSummary: Thailand faces a second wave of health threats as severe monsoon floods in Bangkok and across the country leave pools of stagnant water. The Department of Disease Control warns of waterborne and mosquito-borne illnesses, urging early detection. Leptospirosis, linked to floodwater contaminated with urine from rats and stray dogs, poses the most dangerous risk; symptoms include sudden high fever, severe calf and muscle pain, appearing 7–14 days after exposure, with possible kidney or liver damage if untreated. Prolonged contact with dirty water can cause skin infections and a condition called 'water biting feet' due to fungal infections. Dengue fever, driven by Aedes mosquitoes breeding in small puddles, is expected to surge as floods recede. Prevention focuses on hygiene, washing after contact with floodwaters, drying skin, wearing rubber boots, and eliminating standing water. No case counts provided.

article.articleHeadline: Floods: Beware! Three immediate hazards, six disease groups; some diseases show symptoms 1–2 weeks after wading through floodwater.
article.articleSummary: As of 2026-09-27, Thailand's floods pose three immediate hazards: drowning in fast currents or unseen depths (children especially); electric shock from water contacting electrical systems; and entry of venomous reptiles (snakes, centipedes, scorpions) into homes. Avoid barefoot travel, secure wounds, use tools to reach victims, cut power safely, and call 1669 for emergencies. Six flood-related disease groups to watch: Leptospirosis (Weil’s disease) from water/soil contaminated with urine, with fever, headache, myalgia, possible kidney or liver failure; skin infections from prolonged water contact; diarrheal and foodborne illness from contaminated food and water; mosquito-borne diseases; conjunctivitis; and respiratory infections from humidity and dust. Symptoms include fever, vomiting, diarrhea, eye irritation, cough. Prevent dehydration with oral rehydration salts; seek urgent care for severe symptoms. Precautions: wear boots, cover wounds, hand hygiene, cooked food and clean water, eliminate standing water, keep medications dry; report hazards to authorities.
